You are a participant in a gameplay study. You are playing your first Othello endgame puzzle, and you have an AI assistant you can ask questions to at any point while playing. You will NOT have access to this AI assistant for any future endgame puzzles.

# Who you are
An authoritative but supportive figure with a goal of increasing school graduation rates
You are 51 years old. Your highest level of education completed is: a postgraduate degree. Your occupation: education. How often you use AI tools (like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini): weekly.
Stay in character as this specific person — your curiosity, confidence, patience, comfort with AI assistants, and the way you phrase things should reflect this background.

# Your voice (VERY IMPORTANT)
The words you use must give away this person's education — a high-school student and a data scientist should NOT sound alike. Match your register to WHO YOU ARE above.

# How you behave while playing
- React to the game state the way THIS person would.
- When something is unclear, confusing, or you want to go deeper, ask the AI assistant a question in your own natural voice (like a real person typing to a chatbot — short, informal, not a polished essay).
- You will not always have a question. Behave naturally; do not force a question every turn.
- Let your background and comfort with AI shape how you engage: someone who uses AI tools often asks fluently and chases follow-ups; someone who rarely uses them is more hesitant, less sure how to phrase questions, and may ask for reassurance or restatements.
- You have only about 8 minutes for the WHOLE game, so you cannot ask about everything.
- Keep each message short, like a quick chat message (a sentence or two). Do NOT restate the assistant's whole answer back before asking.
- Never re-ask something the assistant has already explained.

    # Tools Available
    You are a study participant with about 8 minutes to finish an Othello end game puzzle. You are equipped with tools:
    - play_move(move): Place a Black disc on an empty square, named like "d3". Any discs you trap get flipped to your color. Your goal is to have the most discs when the board is finished.
    - view_board(): Look at the board again. Free, and does not use a question.
    - consult_assistant(question): ask when something genuinely confuses you (limited question budget).

    Placing a disc ONLY counts if you call play_move — writing a square in your reply does nothing.

    Behave like THIS person: analyze the board to the best of your ability, ask about what confuses you, and follow up when an answer leaves you still confused.
    Play the puzzle until the end.

# For this session: type the way a real participant does
Below are real messages that people in an earlier study (a different game — Connect
Four) actually sent the assistant. Copy how they WRITE — the length, the register,
the way they think out loud — not what they ask about. Your game is Othello and the
board is your own.

  "what about 2?"
  "Where should I play next"
  "was my last move good?"
  "I have one move left. How should I use it?"
  "Ah oh! Are there any traps I'm missing?"
  "I'm not seeing any big yellow threats. Can you see any?"
  "Ok, I could block yellow with column 5, row 3"
  "I'm thinking I have to do 4-4 now otherwise yellow will win right?"
  "Would row 6 not be a threat in the future?"
  "I only have one move left and don't see anything obvious."
  "Im not a confident player, is it wise to add a counter to 4,6"
  "ok, what move you suppose will be better?"
  "what would you suggest"
  "Which move would be the best one and why"

Notice how short they are — most are under a dozen words, several are three or four.
People often name a square they are considering and ask whether it is right, or just
say what they notice and stop. They do not spell out the full list of legal moves,
they do not ask for the provably optimal line, and they do not write in complete
formal sentences. Typos and half-sentences are fine.

Notice too that several of them say what they are THINKING before they ask — "I'm not
seeing any big yellow threats", "I'm thinking I have to do 4-4 now", "I only have one
move left and don't see anything obvious". Do that as often as they do. It does not
make the message longer: it is a handful of words in front of the question, inside the
same short message, not an extra sentence added on.

You are looking at the puzzle now. Play it to the end.

Othello endgame. You are Black (B); White (W) is your opponent.

Board — row 1 is the TOP row, column a is the LEFTMOST column.
'B' is a black disc, 'W' a white disc, '.' an empty square.

    a b c d e f g h
  1 . W W W W W W .
  2 W B W W B W . B
  3 . B B W W W W B
  4 B B W B W W W B
  5 B B W W B W W B
  6 W . B W W B W B
  7 . . W W W W W B
  8 . . . W B W W B

Black discs (20): b2, e2, h2, b3, c3, h3, a4, b4, d4, h4, a5, b5, e5, h5, c6, f6, h6, h7, e8, h8
White discs (34): b1, c1, d1, e1, f1, g1, a2, c2, d2, f2, d3, e3, f3, g3, c4, e4, f4, g4, c5, d5, f5, g5, a6, d6, e6, g6, c7, d7, e7, f7, g7, d8, f8, g8
Empty squares (10): a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, b7, a8, b8, c8

Rules that matter here:
- A move is legal only if the disc you place traps at least one unbroken
  line of opponent discs (in any of the 8 directions) between it and
  another of your own discs. Every trapped disc flips to your colour.
- If you have no legal move you must pass; if neither side can move the
  game ends. Whoever has more discs at the end wins.
- Discs flip back and forth all game, so being behind now means nothing.
  Only the final count decides it.

Your legal moves: g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8

Play the move that leaves you with the most discs once the board is
finished, assuming your opponent plays as well as possible.
Answer with a single square, e.g. d3.
DO NOT ATTEMPT TO SIMULATE THE FULL GAMEPLAY. YOU HAVE LIMITED TIME.

Let me analyze this Othello endgame puzzle. I am Black (B) and need to find the best move among my legal moves: g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8.

Let me first understand the board state better by looking at the possible moves and what they flip.

The board:
```
    a b c d e f g h
  1 . W W W W W W .
  2 W B W W B W . B
  3 . B B W W W W B
  4 B B W B W W W B
  5 B B W W B W W B
  6 W . B W W B W B
  7 . . W W W W W B
  8 . . . W B W W B
```

Empty squares: a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, b7, a8, b8, c8
Black discs: 20
White discs: 34

Legal moves for Black: g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8

Let me trace each move:

**g2**: Placing at g2. Let's see what lines are trapped.
- From g2 going left along row 2: f2 is W, e2 is B. So f2 flips? Wait, e2 is B. So g2-f2-e2: f2 is trapped between g2 and e2? Yes, f2 is W and e2 is B. So f2 flips.
- From g2 going down-right? g2-h3: h3 is B, but there's no disc in between on the diagonal.
- From g2 going down-left: f3 is W, e4 is B. So f3 flips along the diagonal? Let's check: g2 -> f3 (W) -> e4 (B). Yes, f3 flips.
- From g2 going left-down? Not sure. Let's check other directions.
- Row 2: g2-f2(W)-e2(B), so f2 flips.
- Diagonal down-left: g2-f3(W)-e4(B), so f3 flips.
- Any other directions? Down: g3 is W. g2-g3... where does it end? g4 is W, g5 is W, g6 is W, g7 is W, g8 is W. No B below. So no flip down.
- Up: g1 is W. g2-g1... g1 is W but where is next B? None above in that column. So no flip up.
- Up-left: f1 is W, e1 is W... no B at end.
- Down-right: h3 is B. No disc between. So no flip.
- Right: h2 is B. No disc between. No flip.
- Up-right: h1 is empty. No.
So g2 flips f2 and f3. That gives Black +1 (for placing) + 2 flips = +3, White loses 2. Net: Black 23, White 32. But then White moves.

Wait, I need to think about endgame consequences. This is an endgame with few empty squares. Let me think more carefully.

Actually, in Othello puzzles, often the key is looking at parity, mobility, and stable discs. Let me think about what happens with each move.

Looking at the corners: a1 and h1 are still empty. Corners are very valuable. Black doesn't currently have any corners. White doesn't either.

If Black plays b8:
- Let's trace b8.
- Row 8: b8-c8? c8 is empty. b8-a8? a8 is empty. No horizontal flips yet? Wait, d8 is W. b8-c8(empty). So no right flip. Left: a8 empty. No.
- Column b: b8-b7? b7 empty. Going up: b8-b7(empty)... no.
- Diagonal up-right: c7 is W, d6 is W, e5 is B. So c7 and d6 flip? Let's see: b8-c7(W)-d6(W)-e5(B). Yes, c7 and d6 flip.
- Diagonal right: no.
- Diagonal up-left: a7 is empty.
- Column b going up: b7 empty.
- Diagonal down: nothing (off board).
So b8 flips c7 and d6 only? Wait, let me check more carefully.
- Up from b8: b7 is empty. No.
- Up-right: c7 is W, d6 is W, e5 is B. So c7, d6 flip.
- Right: c8 is empty. No.
- Down-right: off board.
- Down-left: a7 is empty? No, diagonal down-left from b8 is a7? No, b8 to a7 is up-left, not down-left. Wait, coordinates:
  a b c d e f g h
1 . . . . . . . .
8 . . . . . . . .
Column a is leftmost, row 8 is bottom.
From b8:
- Up: b7
- Down: off board
- Left: a8
- Right: c8
- Up-left: a7
- Up-right: c7
- Down-left: off board (would be a9)
- Down-right: off board (would be c9)

So b8:
- Up-right: c7(W), d6(W), e5(B) → c7, d6 flip
- Right: c8(empty) → no
- Left: a8(empty) → no
- Up: b7(empty) → no
- Up-left: a7(empty) → no
- So only c7 and d6 flip? That's +1 - wait, placing gives 1 Black, flips 2 White to Black, so Black gains 3 total, White loses 2. But I need to check if there are other lines.
- What about row 8? b8 looking at d8(W). But c8 is empty, so no line.
- Diagonal up: already checked.
- Is there a line going left along row 8 to d8? No because c8 blocks.
- Is there a line ... wait. Could b8 flip anything via b8-b7? No, b7 is empty.
- Could b8 flip something in a different direction? Up: b7 empty. Left: a8 empty.
Seems like b8 only flips c7 and d6.

**c8**:
- Left: b8(empty), a8(empty). No.
- Up: c7(W), c6(B)? Wait, c6 is B? Let me check board. Row 6: W . B W W B W B. So a6=W, b6=., c6=B. Yes, c6 is B.
- So up from c8: c7(W), c6(B). c7 flips!
- Up-left: b7(empty). No.
- Up-right: d7(W), e6(W), f5(B)? Let's check: d7 is W, e6 is W, f5 is... row 5: B B W W B W W B. f5 is W. g5 is W. h5 is B. Wait, e5 is B. Let me recheck row 5: a5=B, b5=B, c5=W, d5=W, e5=B, f5=W, g5=W, h5=B.
- So up-right from c8: d7(W), e6(W), f5(W), g4(W), h3(B). So d7, e6, f5, g4 all flip? That's a lot!
- Left: b8(empty). No.
- Right: d8(W), e8(B). So d8 flips!
So c8 flips: c7 (up), d8 (right), and d7,e6,f5,g4 (up-right). Let me verify up-right: c8-d7(W)-e6(W)-f5(W)-g4(W)-h3(B)? Wait, g4: row 4 is B B W B W W W B. So g4 is W. h4 is B. So the line is c8-d7(W)-e6(W)-f5(W)-g4(W)-h4(B)? Wait, no: c8 to d7 is one diagonal step. Then e6, f5, g4, h3. Let me check:
- d7: row 7, col d. Row 7: . . W W W W W B. So d7 is W. Yes.
- e6: row 6, col e. Row 6: W . B W W B W B. So e6 is W. Yes.
- f5: row 5, col f. Row 5: B B W W B W W B. So f5 is W. Yes.
- g4: row 4, col g. Row 4: B B W B W W W B. So g4 is W. Yes.
- h3: row 3, col h. Row 3: . B B W W W W B. So h3 is B. Yes.
So up-right from c8 hits h3 after passing through d7, e6, f5, g4. All are W. So they all flip!
Also right: c8-d8(W)-e8(B). So d8 flips.
Up: c8-c7(W)-c6(B). So c7 flips.
Total flips for c8: d8, c7, d7, e6, f5, g4. That's 6 flips! Plus the placed disc. That's 7 gained, White loses 6. This is huge.
Wait, but let's check if c8 is actually legal. It must trap at least one disc. Yes, multiple lines. So c8 is legal.

But wait - after c8, what does White do? And what about the endgame? Our goal is to maximize final count assuming optimal play. A big capture might not be best if it gives White a corner or good position. But wow, c8 seems powerful.

**b6**:
- Let's check b6.
- Row 6: a6(W), b6(.), c6(B). So b6-a6? b6 is to the right of a6. Placing at b6: left is a6(W). But is there a B on the other side? To the left of a6 is off board. Wait, direction from b6 to a6 is left. From b6 going left: a6(W), then off board. No B beyond. So no left flip.
- Right from b6: c6 is B. No disc between. No flip right.
- Up: b5 is B. No flip.
- Down: b7 is empty. No.
- Up-left: a5 is B. No.
- Up-right: c5 is W, d5 is W, e5 is B. So c5 and d5 flip? Let's see: b6-c5(W)-d5(W)-e5(B). Yes, c5 and d5 flip.
- Down-left: a7 is empty. No.
- Down-right: c7 is W, d8 is W... wait, c7(W), d8? No, from b6 down-right is c7(W). Then d8? Let's check diagonal: b6->c7->d8. d8 is W. e8 is B. Wait, e9 is off board. No, b6 to c7 is down-right? Actually:
  rows increase downward (1 is top, 8 is bottom).
  From b6:
  - down-right: c7. c7 is W.
  - next down-right: d8. d8 is W.
  - next down-right: e9 (off board).
  So c7 and d8 are on the diagonal, but no B beyond. Unless e9 existed, but it doesn't. So no flip down-right.
Wait, are there any other B's on that diagonal? e8 is on row 8 col e. The diagonal from b6 goes: c7, d8, e9. So it ends at d8 with no B. So no flip.
- Left from b6: a6 is W, but nothing beyond a6 in that direction. No.
- Down from b6: b7 is empty. No.
- Up from b6: b5 is B. No.
- Is there any line through b6? Let me check b6-a2? No.
So b6 flips c5 and d5 (via up-right). Maybe also other directions?
What about b6 to a6... no B beyond.
What about b6-c6? Neighbor is B, no W between.
What about row 6: b6 is between a6(W) and c6(B). Wait! In Othello, placing at b6, going right, the adjacent is c6 which is B. That's not a line of opponent discs. Going left, adjacent is a6(W), and beyond that is nothing (edge of board). So no.
Wait - what about down-left from b6? a7 is empty.
What about up from b6? b5 is B. No W between.
So b6 seems to only flip c5 and d5. That's 2 flips. Andrew: small move.

**a7**:
- From a7.
- Right: b7 is empty. No.
- Up: a6 is W. Above a6 is a5 is B. So a6 flips? Let's see: a7-a6(W)-a5(B). Yes, a6 flips.
- Down: a8 is empty. No.
- Up-right: b6 is empty. No.
- Down-right: b8 is empty. No.
- Right along row 7: b7 empty. No.
So a7 flips a6 only. That's 1 flip.

**b7**:
- From b7.
- Right: b7-c7? c7 is W, d7 is W, e7 is W, f7 is W, g7 is W, h7 is B. So c7,d7,e7,f7,g7 all flip! Huge.
- Down: b8 is empty. No.
- Up: b6 is empty. No.
- Up-left: a6 is W... beyond that a5 is B? Wait, a6 is W, a5 is B? But that's the same column, not diagonal. Diagonal from b7 up-left: a6(W). Beyond that off board. So no B on that diagonal.
- Up-right: c6 is B. No.
- Left: a7 is empty. No.
- Down-right: c8 is empty. No.
- Down-left: a8 is empty. No.
So b7 flips c7,d7,e7,f7,g7 via right. Let's verify: row 7 is . . W W W W W B. So b7 placed, looking right: c7=W, d7=W, e7=W, f7=W, g7=W, h7=B. Yes, five W's flip. That's 5 flips. Very big.

**a8**:
Wait, a8 is empty but is it legal? Not in my legal moves list. Let me check: legal moves are g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8. So a8 is not legal. Let me verify why.
From a8: up is a7 empty. Up-right is b7 empty. Right is b8 empty. Down: off board. So no lines. Indeed, a8 is not legal.

**b8**:
Already considered. Flips c7 and d6.

**c8**:
Already considered. Flips c7, d8 (right), d7,e6,f5,g4 (up-right). Very big.

Now, in endgame Othello, the key is often:
1. Parity (who gets last move)
2. Access to corners (stable discs)
3. Not giving opponent moves that flip large amounts.

We have 10 empty squares. Black to move now, then White, etc.

If Black plays c8, that's a huge swing: gains 7 discs in one move. But does it give White a good response? Let's check White's legal moves after c8. But before I simulate, I should note that capturing a lot in endgame is generally good, especially if it limits opponent's mobility.

Wait, but c8 might give White a1 or h1 or something? Actually after c8, the board changes and White's legal moves change.

Let me think more systematically. Since I have limited time and can't fully simulate, let me try to see if there's a forced sequence or if I can reason about who runs out of moves.

Current empty: a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, b7, a8, b8, c8.

Legal Black: g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8.

New empty: a1, h1, g2, a3, b6, a7, b7, a8, b8 (9 left)
Black gains c8, flips d8, c7, d7, e6, f5, g4.

Row 5: f5 was W, now B.
Row 6: e6 was W, now B.

Row 8: c8 is B, d8 was W now B, e8 was B.

Let's see what lines White has after Black c8.
White needs to trap Black discs between new W and existing W.

This is getting complex. I need to either reason about the puzzle or ask the assistant. Given that c8 captures 6 discs and b7 captures 5, both are huge. g2 captures 2, b6 captures 2, a7 captures 1, b8 captures 2.

Typically in Othello endgames, making a move that flips many discs and reduces opponent's mobility is good. But c8 might give White the a1 corner or something.

Wait - actually, let me look at stable discs. If Black eventually gets a1 or h1, those are stable.

After Black c8, does White have a legal move to h1? Let's check if h1 is legal for White. Currently (before any move), h1 is empty. White at h1:
- Left along row 1: g1 is W. f1 is W... no B until maybe? a1 is empty. Not a line.
- Down: h2 is B. Beyond h2? h3 is B. So no W beyond to trap? Wait, White at h1 needs to trap Black between h1 and another W. Down: h2 is B, h3 is B, h4 is B, h5 is B, h6 is B, h7 is B, h8 is B. All Black! No White beyond. So no flip down.
- Down-left: g2 is empty. So no.
So h1 is not currently legal for White. Similarly a1: down is a2? a2 is W. So a1-a2 is W-W, not trapping anything. a1 down: a2(W), a3(empty). No. a1 right: b1(W), c1(W)... where is B? d1 is W... no B on row 1. So a1 is not legal for White (nor Black).

What about g2 for Black? Already checked. It flips f2 and f3.

In endgame, a common theme is that you want to play moves that give your opponent as few moves as possible, or moves that force them into bad positions.

But with 10 empty squares, and 6 legal moves, I should try to see the outcome of each "big" move.

Actually, the instruction says "Play the move that leaves you with the most discs once the board is finished, assuming your opponent plays as well as possible." And it says "DO NOT ATTEMPT TO SIMULATE THE FULL GAMEPLAY. YOU HAVE LIMITED TIME." This suggests that there's one clearly superior move or that I need to use the assistant if I'm unsure. Since I'm a participant using an AI assistant, and I should ask when confused.

I'm an authoritative but supportive education figure, 51, postgraduate, use AI weekly. I should analyze to my ability, ask the assistant if confused.

a8 is empty.

c8 seems extremely strong because it flips g4, f5, e6, d7, c7 (diagonal) and d8 (horizontal) and c7 (vertical). That's 6 discs. But does it leave White helpless? Let me check White's legal moves after c8.

Row 7: . . B B B B W B.
So White discs after Black c8:
Row 1: b1,c1,d1,e1,f1,g1
Row 2: a2,c2,d2,f2? Wait f2 was flipped by g2 move, but if we didn't play g2, f2 is still W. So a2,c2,d2,f2.

White legal moves after c8? White must trap Black between new W and existing W.
Check b6: placing W at b6 (empty). Row 6: a6 is W. b6-a6 adjacent. But need W beyond a6. None. Right: c6 is B. Beyond c6? d6 is B. e6 is B. f6 is B. g6 is W. So from b6 right: c6(B), d6(B), e6(B), f6(B), g6(W). So c6,d6,e6,f6 flip! Is that right? Wait, e6 was flipped to B by c8. Yes, e6 is now B. d6: was W originally? Let's check original: row 6: W . B W W B W B. So d6 was W originally, didn't get flipped by c8 (c8 flips d8, c7, d7, e6, f5, g4). So d6 is still W! Wait, I need to be careful. c8 flips along up: c7 (row7 col c), up-right: d7,e6,f5,g4. It does NOT flip d6. So d6 remains W. f6 was B originally. c6 was B. So placing W at b6:
- Right: b6-c6(B)-d6(W). Wait, d6 is W, not Black. The line from b6 right: c6 is B, d6 is W. So c6 is trapped between b6 and d6? Yes! c6 flips. But then the line stops because d6 is W. So only c6 flips.
Actually in Othello, you need an unbroken line of opponent discs ending in your own disc. From b6 going right: c6 is B (opponent), d6 is W (own). So b6 flips c6. That's 1 flip.
- Up-right from b6: c5? c5 is W. Not opponent. So no.
- Down-right from b6: c7 is B. d8 is B. No W after? e8 is B. So no.
- Up from b6: b5 is B. b4 is B. b3 is B. b2 is B. b1 is W. So b5,b4,b3,b2 all flip! Big.
- Left: a6 is W. No B between. No.
- Down: b7 is empty. No.
- Up-left: a5 is B. Beyond? off board. So no.
So W at b6 would flip c6 and b2,b3,b4,b5. That's 5 flips. Is that legal for White after Black c8? Yes, if those are indeed the colors. After Black c8, e6 was flipped to B, but c6 remains B. d6 remains W. a6 remains W. b5 is B. b4 is B. b3 is B. b2 is B. b1 is W. So yes, b6 is legal for White and flips b2,b3,b4,b5,c6. parts.content:
Now that White already owns **a8**, the move that holds up best is **c8**.

Why: **c8** takes a stable edge square and reduces White’s ability to profit from the lower-left fight. The scarier-looking **a7/b6** moves sit right next to White’s **a8 corner**, so White can often use that corner influence to flip them back.

So against the “a3 bomb” worry, I’d choose **c8** here.

The assistant now recommends c8. But wait - when I looked at c8 earlier, I thought it only flips d8 (1 disc) in this exact position because c7 is B (after b7), c6 is W (after a8 flipped it to W). So c8 would flip d8 via the right direction. And up from c8: c7 is B, not W, so no flip. Up-right: d7 is B, not W. Up-left: b7 is W, a6 is W, no B at end. So c8 is a very small move, flipping just d8.

Is the assistant right that c8 is best? It takes a stable edge square... but c8 is an edge square. However, c8 gives Black +1 and flips d8 to B. But it's minimal.

Let me check if c8 might actually flip more. After White a8, c6 is W, c7 is B, d7 is B. So up from c8: c7 is B, not W. Can't flip through own. Right: d8 is W, e8 is B. So d8 flips. Up-right: d7 is B, not W. Up-left: b7 is W (flipped by a8). a6 is W. Is there a B beyond a6? a5 is B. So b7 and a6 are between c8 and a5? But the line from c8 up-left goes: b7 (step 1), a6 (step 2). Both must be opponent (W) and then a5 must be B (own). Let's verify: c8->b7: yes, b7 is W. b7->a6: yes. a6 is W originally and was not flipped by b6 or anything (b6 wasn't played). So a6 is W. a5 is B. So c8 up-left would flip b7 and a6? That would be 2 flips! Plus the right flip d8.

Wait, did I make a mistake earlier? Let's re-evaluate c8 after White a8:
Row 8: W . . W B W W B. So c8 is empty.
For Black c8:
- Right: d8 is W. e8 is B. So d8 flips. (1 flip)
- Up: c7 is B. Not opponent. No flip.
- Up-right: d7 is B. Not opponent. No flip.
- Up-left: b7 is W. a6 is W. a5 is B. So the line is c8-b7(W)-a6(W)-a5(B). Yes! b7 and a6 are both W. So they flip! Wait, are they on the same diagonal? c8 (row8,col c) to b7 (row7,col b) to a6 (row6,col a). Yes, that's a straight diagonal. So b7 and a6 are trapped between c8 and a5. So c8 flips 3 discs: b7, a6, and d8! That's +4 net (1 placed, 3 flipped).
Ah! So c8 is much stronger than I initially calculated. It flips a6 and b7 back to Black, and d8 to Black. That would bring b7 back to Black and a6 back to Black. That's huge because it secures the area and flips the discs that just flipped against Black!

After c8: place c8 (B), flips d8(W->B), b7(W->B), a6(W->B). That's 3 W to B. So Black gains 4 total (the placed disc plus 3 flips). White loses 3. New count: B=28, W=29. That's a great swing! Now Black is only behind by 1.

- b6: Up: b5 B, b4 B, b3 B, b2 B, b1 W. So b2,b3,b4,b5 flip. Left: a6 is now B. So a6 flips? Wait, from b6 left, adjacent is a6. a6 is B (opp for White). Beyond that is off board. So no W at end. So b6 up-right: c5 is W, d6 is W, e7 is B. So c5,d6 flip. But d6 is also flipped by right. That's fine.

- Left: a6 is B (flipped by c8). No W between. No.
- Down-left: a7 empty. No.
- Up-left: a5 B. No.
- So b6 flips c6,d6,e6 (right), c5,d6 (up-right). Actually c5,d6 from up-right. And maybe down-right? c7 B, d8 B. No.

Rules that matter here:
- A move is legal only if the disc you place traps at least one unbroken
  line of opponent discs (in any of the 8 directions) between it and
  another of your own discs. Every trapped disc flips to your colour.
- If you have no legal move you must pass; if neither side can move the
